summary.text: Lesson 1-4 of enVision Math Grade 4: rounding to any place using the number line's halfway point or the digit rule. Covers picking the rounding digit, the 5-or-more rule, what range of numbers rounds to a given benchmark, and spotting the wrong-place rounding error.

why.text: Rounding is the tool the next topic runs on — every estimate before an exact answer in Topic 2 is a rounding move. It is also the first place math asks you to reason about a RANGE of possible numbers instead of one, which is a genuinely new kind of thinking.

objectives.text: Round any number up to one million to a named place
Use the halfway point on a number line to justify a rounding
Find the range of numbers that round to a given benchmark
Spot a correct rounding of the wrong place

parentNote.text: Built from the HW 1-4 sheet. The error to watch for is rounding the WRONG PLACE correctly — her sheet and this quiz both feature it, because it is the top scoring leak on rounding tests. The other stretch here is un-rounding: 'the announcer said about 40,000 — what could the real number be?' Those range questions are where the level 3s live. School rule applied throughout: 5 rounds up.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz in one sitting. Underline the place word in every question before answering.

cards.def:
**Rounding replaces a number with the nearest benchmark — the nearest multiple of 10, 100, 1,000 and so on.**
• 181,376 to the nearest thousand is 181,000, because it is closer to 181,000 than to 182,000.
• A rounded number trades exactness for ease.

**A number below the halfway point rounds down; at halfway or above, it rounds up.**
• Between 181,000 and 182,000 the halfway point is 181,500.
• 181,376 sits below it, so it rounds down.
cards.hint: Picture the number line. Which benchmark is it actually closer to?

cards.def:
**Find the rounding place, look ONE digit to its right: 5 or more rounds up, less than 5 leaves it alone. Then zero out everything to the right.**
• Round 181,376 to the nearest hundred: the 3 is the rounding digit, the 7 to its right says round up — 181,400.
• The number-line picture and the digit rule always agree; the rule is just faster.

**Many different numbers round to the same benchmark.**
• Every number from 84,500 up to 85,499 rounds to 85,000 at the nearest thousand.
• That is why you cannot un-round: the original is gone.
cards.hint: A rounded number is a neighbourhood, not an address.

cards.def:
**The place you round to sets how rough the estimate is.**
• 46,512 is 47,000 to the nearest thousand but 46,500 to the nearest hundred.
• Rougher is faster; finer is closer. Which you want depends on the question.

questions.hint: The digit to the right of the thousands place makes the call.
steps: The rounding place is the thousands: the 3.
Look one digit right: 4. Less than 5, so the 3 stays.
Zero out the rest: 73,000.

ex.main: **73,000.** The 481 tail is below the halfway point of 500, so the number rounds down.
ex.tip: Only the single digit to the right of the rounding place matters. The rest is noise.

questions.q: Round 249,731 to the nearest hundred thousand.
steps: The rounding place is the hundred thousands: the 2.
One digit right: 4. Less than 5, so the 2 stays.
Everything else becomes zero: 200,000.

ex.main: **200,000.** Close call — 249,731 is only 269 short of rounding the other way at 250,000.
ex.tip: The bigger the rounding place, the more gets thrown away. Here almost fifty thousand vanished.

questions.q: What is the halfway point between 56,000 and 57,000?
steps: The two benchmarks are 56,000 and 57,000, a gap of 1,000.
Half of 1,000 is 500.
So the halfway point is 56,000 + 500 = 56,500.

ex.main: **56,500.** Anything below it rounds to 56,000; anything at or above it rounds to 57,000.
ex.tip: The halfway point always ends in 5 followed by zeros. That shape is the tell.

questions.q: Round 46,512 to the nearest thousand AND to the nearest hundred. Which pair is right?
questions.hint: Two separate roundings of the same number. Do them one at a time.
steps: Nearest thousand: rounding digit 6, next digit 5 — round up. 47,000.
Nearest hundred: rounding digit 5, next digit 1 — stays. 46,500.
One number, two answers, because the rounding place changed.

ex.main: **47,000 and 46,500.** Notice they even moved in different directions — the thousand rounded up while the hundred stayed.
ex.tip: Always restate WHICH place you are rounding to. The same number gives different answers.

questions.q: A stadium announcer says attendance was "about 40,000", rounded to the nearest ten thousand. Which could be the actual attendance?
questions.hint: Find the full range of numbers that round to 40,000.
steps: To round to 40,000 at the nearest ten thousand, a number must be from 35,000 up to 44,999.
41,377 is inside that range.

ex.main: **41,377.** Un-rounding gives a range, never a single answer — the exact count is unrecoverable.
ex.tip: The range for a benchmark runs from its halfway point below to just before its halfway point above.

questions.q: Three parks report visitors: Elm 218,943, Oak 224,500, Cedar 214,067. Rounded to the nearest ten thousand, which parks show the SAME number?
opts: Elm and Oak — both 220,000
Elm and Cedar — both 220,000
Oak and Cedar — both 210,000
All three round to different numbers
questions.hint: Round each one separately, then compare the results.
steps: Elm 218,943: thousands digit 8 rounds the ten thousands up — 220,000.
Oak 224,500: thousands digit 4 leaves it — 220,000.
Cedar 214,067: thousands digit 4 leaves it too — 210,000.
Elm and Oak both show 220,000; Cedar stands apart.

ex.main: **Elm and Oak, both 220,000.** Rounding erases differences — two parks over 5,000 visitors apart become identical.
ex.tip: When rounded numbers match, the originals can still be far apart. That is the cost of rounding.

questions.q: A number rounds to 85,000 at the nearest thousand. What is the SMALLEST it could be?
questions.hint: The bottom of the neighbourhood is the halfway point below.
steps: Numbers round to 85,000 from both sides.
From below, the first number that rounds UP to 85,000 is the halfway point: 84,500.
One less, 84,499, rounds down to 84,000 instead.
So the smallest possibility is 84,500.

ex.main: **84,500.** The neighbourhood of 85,000 runs from 84,500 through 85,499.
ex.tip: Smallest-possible and largest-possible questions are asking for the two ends of the range.

questions.q: Kenji says 296,480 rounded to the nearest thousand is 300,000. What went wrong?
opts: He rounded to the nearest hundred thousand instead — nearest thousand gives 296,000
Nothing, he is correct
He should have gotten 297,000
He rounded down when he should have rounded up
questions.hint: Check which place his answer is actually rounded to.
steps: Nearest thousand: rounding digit is the 6, next digit is 4, so it stays — 296,000.
300,000 is what you get rounding to the nearest hundred thousand.
Kenji did a correct rounding — of the wrong place.
The fix is not new arithmetic; it is re-reading which place was asked for.

ex.main: **He rounded to the wrong place.** His arithmetic was fine and his answer is still wrong — precision about the question is part of the skill.
ex.tip: Wrong-place rounding is the most common error on these tests. Underline the place word in the question.

questions.q: A librarian rounds the book count to the nearest hundred for a poster and gets 12,300. A visitor asks whether the library could have exactly 12,349 books. What is the right answer?
opts: Yes — 12,349 rounds to 12,300, so it is possible
No — 12,349 rounds to 12,350
No — the count must end in zero
Yes — any number near 12,300 is possible, even 12,251
questions.hint: Round 12,349 to the nearest hundred and see if it lands on 12,300.
steps: Nearest hundred for 12,349: rounding digit 3, next digit 4, stays — 12,300.
So 12,349 is inside the 12,300 neighbourhood, which runs 12,250 to 12,349.
It is in fact the LARGEST number that still rounds to 12,300.
So yes, the library could have exactly 12,349 books.

ex.main: **Yes.** A rounded number is consistent with a whole range of exact counts — reasoning about that range is the real skill.
ex.tip: Note the neighbour: 12,350 would round UP to 12,400. One book changes the poster.

questions.q: If a number rounds UP when rounded to the nearest ten, does it always round up to the nearest hundred too?
opts: No — 146 rounds up to 150 at the nearest ten but down to 100 at the nearest hundred
Yes — rounding direction is a property of the number
Yes — bigger places always follow smaller ones
No — it always rounds down instead
questions.hint: Find one number that goes up at tens and down at hundreds. One example settles it.
steps: Take 146. Nearest ten: ones digit 6, round up — 150.
Nearest hundred: tens digit 4, stays — 100.
Same number, up at one place, down at another.
One counterexample is all it takes to defeat an "always" claim.

ex.main: **No — 146 rounds up to 150 but down to 100.** Each rounding place makes its own decision from its own neighbour digit.
ex.tip: To break any "always" statement, hunt for one counterexample. That is a full proof.
